notes.0: The stage and the slide hold the specimen in position. They do not make the specimen look any bigger. Think about which parts contain lenses.
notes.2: The arm and the base support the microscope and are used to carry it. They contain no lenses, so they cannot magnify the specimen.
notes.3: The light and the mirror make the specimen bright enough to see. Making the view brighter is not the same as making the specimen look bigger.

why.right: A microscope magnifies a specimen because light passes through two lenses that each make the image bigger.
wrong: A microscope magnifies a specimen because the stage pushes the specimen much closer to the eye.
A microscope magnifies a specimen because a brighter light makes the specimen grow larger.

explain: The eyepiece is the lens you look through. The objective lens is the lens near the specimen. Together they make things look bigger.

notes.0: Making the image bigger is done by the lenses. The base is the flat bottom part and contains no lens.
notes.1: Holding the slide is the job of the stage clips on the stage. The base is lower down, at the bottom of the microscope.
notes.3: Light is directed by the mirror or lamp near the stage. The base is the heavy flat part the microscope stands on.

explain: The base is the flat bottom part. It stops the microscope from falling over when you put it on a table.

notes.0: The light knob changes how bright the view is. Brightness does not make a blurry image sharp. Focusing needs a knob that moves the stage or lens.
notes.2: The stage clip only holds the slide still. It is not turned and does not change the focus.
notes.3: The mirror directs light onto the specimen. It changes brightness, not sharpness. Look for a knob that moves the stage by tiny amounts.

why.right: The fine adjustment knob is used last because it moves the stage by very small amounts to sharpen the image.
wrong: The fine adjustment knob is used last because it makes the light brighter until the image becomes sharp.
The fine adjustment knob is used last because it moves the stage by large amounts to find the specimen.

explain: The fine adjustment knob moves slowly and carefully. You use it to make the image clear and sharp after you see it first.

notes.0: All magnifications use the same knobs and steps. The reason is about how much of the slide can be seen at once.
notes.2: The magnification used does not change how safe the microscope is for the eyes. Think about how big an area of the slide is visible.
notes.3: Low magnification does not make colours brighter. Think about how much of the slide is visible and how that helps to locate the specimen.

why.right: Low magnification is used first because it shows a larger area, so the specimen is easier to find.
wrong: Low magnification is used first because it shows more detail, so the cells are easier to study.
Low magnification is used first because it makes the specimen larger, so it fills the whole view.

explain: Low magnification shows a bigger area of the slide. This makes it easier to find the specimen and move it to the middle of the view before using a higher magnification.

notes.0: The light is there so the specimen can be seen. Heating would damage a specimen, especially living cells.
notes.1: Making the specimen look bigger is the job of the lenses. The light does not change the size of the image.
notes.3: Colouring a specimen is done with a stain such as iodine or methylene blue, added when the slide is made. The light itself adds no colour.

why.right: A microscope needs a light source because light must pass through the thin specimen to reach the eye.
wrong: A microscope needs a light source because light makes the specimen bigger before it reaches the lenses.
A microscope needs a light source because light warms the specimen so the cells move into view.

explain: The light passes through the specimen. Without light, you cannot see anything under the microscope.

notes.0: Taking a microscope apart can damage the lenses and other parts. It is carried whole, held at its strongest points.
notes.1: The eyepiece can slide out of the tube, so the microscope could fall. Think about which parts are strong enough to take its weight.
notes.3: Wrapping it does not stop it from slipping or falling. What matters is how it is held while it is carried.

why.right: A microscope is carried by the arm and base because these strong parts can hold its full weight safely.
wrong: A microscope is carried by the eyepiece because the eyepiece is the strongest part of the microscope.
A microscope is carried in pieces because the parts are lighter and safer when carried apart.

explain: Always hold the arm and support the base with your hand. This keeps it safe and stops it from getting damaged.

notes.0: How the microscope looks does not matter. Think about what dirt on the glass parts does to the image.
notes.2: Dust on a microscope does not affect the building. Think about what dust on the lenses does to the view.
notes.3: Cleaning helps, but no instrument works forever. The main reason is linked to what is seen through the lenses.

why.right: Microscope lenses are kept clean because dirt blocks light and makes the image blurry.
wrong: Microscope lenses are kept clean because dirt makes the specimen look bigger than it is.
Microscope lenses are kept clean because dirt changes the colour of the cells on the slide.

explain: If dust and dirt are on the lenses, they block light and make the image blurry. Clean lenses give a clear image.

notes.0: Nothing on the stage makes the slide bigger. Only the lenses make the image look bigger.
notes.2: Light is directed by the mirror or lamp. The stage clip is a small metal holder on the stage.
notes.3: Lenses are cleaned with lens paper. The stage clip sits on the stage, so think about what it touches.

explain: The stage clip is a metal holder. It keeps your slide from moving around when you are looking at it.

notes.0: The stage is fixed and needs nothing to hold it. The coverslip goes on the slide, directly over the specimen.
notes.2: A coverslip is flat glass, not a lens. It does not make the specimen look bigger.
notes.3: A coverslip is a thin piece of glass and has no connection to the light. Think about where it is placed on the slide.

why.right: A coverslip is placed over the specimen because it keeps the specimen flat and protects it from dust.
wrong: A coverslip is placed over the specimen because it acts as a lens and makes the specimen bigger.
A coverslip is placed over the specimen because it holds the slide firmly in place on the stage.

explain: A coverslip is a thin piece of glass. You put it on top of the specimen to protect it and flatten it for better viewing.

notes.0: Stains are not used to kill specimens. Many cell parts are almost colourless, so think about how a stain changes what can be seen.
notes.1: A stain does not change the size of the cells. It changes how clearly parts of the cell show up.
notes.3: A stain does not keep the specimen fresh. Think about why colourless cell parts are hard to see.

why.right: Stains are added to cells because many cell parts are colourless and hard to see without colour.
wrong: Stains are added to cells because the dye makes the cells swell to a larger size.
Stains are added to cells because the dye stops the cells from drying out on the slide.

explain: Stains add colour to the structures inside cells. Coloured structures are much easier to see than clear, colourless ones.

notes.0: A battery is also called a cell, but in biology the word means something different. Think about what living things are made of.
notes.2: Many cells do form tissues, but this does not define a cell. Not every living thing has tissues. Think about what every living thing has.
notes.3: A cell is living, not a piece of rock. Think about what all living things are made of.

explain: A cell is the basic building block of all living things. All organisms are made of one or more cells.

notes.0: The cell membrane controls what enters and leaves the cell. It does not control everything the cell does.
notes.2: The cytoplasm is where many reactions happen, but it does not direct them. Think about the part that holds the cell's instructions.
notes.3: The vacuole stores water and dissolved substances. Storage does not control the cell's activities.

why.right: The nucleus controls the cell because it holds the instructions that direct the cell's activities and growth.
wrong: The nucleus controls the cell because it lets substances in and out across the cell edge.
The nucleus controls the cell because it stores the water and food the cell uses.

explain: The nucleus controls the activities of the cell. It holds the instructions that decide what the cell does and how it grows.

notes.0: The cell wall is a separate rigid layer found in plant cells. The cytoplasm is found inside the cell.
notes.2: The green parts of a plant cell are the chloroplasts. The cytoplasm itself is not coloured.
notes.3: The outer layer of an animal cell is the cell membrane. The cytoplasm is found inside that layer.

explain: Cytoplasm is a watery gel that fills the cell. Chemical reactions happen here to keep the cell alive.

notes.0: The membrane does not make the cell bigger. Think about the membrane's position at the edge of the cell.
notes.2: The membrane does not produce energy. Its position around the cell gives a clue to its job.
notes.3: Storage is the job of the vacuole. The membrane is the thin layer around the outside of the cell.

explain: The cell membrane is a protective layer. It decides what substances can enter and leave the cell.

notes.0: Animal cells also have a cell membrane, and it is thin and flexible. It cannot hold a plant cell stiff.
notes.1: Both plant and animal cells have a nucleus. It controls the cell but does not make it stiff.
notes.3: Chloroplasts are found only in plant cells, but their job is to make food. They do not help the plant stand up straight.

why.right: Plant cells keep a fixed shape because a tough, rigid cell wall surrounds the cell membrane.
wrong: Plant cells keep a fixed shape because the nucleus pushes outwards on every side of the cell.
Plant cells keep a fixed shape because chloroplasts form a hard layer just under the membrane.

explain: The cell wall is a tough, rigid layer outside the cell membrane. It gives plant cells their fixed shape and makes them stiff.

notes.0: Water is mainly stored in the vacuole. Chloroplasts are green and contain chlorophyll, which absorbs light.
notes.1: Controlling the cell is the job of the nucleus. Chloroplasts are green structures that absorb light.
notes.3: Chloroplasts do not break down waste. Think about what plants do with light energy.

why.right: Chloroplasts make food because they contain chlorophyll, which absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.
wrong: Chloroplasts make food because they take in ready-made food from the soil through the roots.
Chloroplasts make food because they turn waste from the cell into sugar for the plant.

explain: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which absorbs light. The plant uses this light energy to make food (glucose) by photosynthesis.

notes.0: Vacuoles do not move cells. A vacuole is a space inside the cell filled with liquid.
notes.2: The vacuole does not surround or protect the nucleus. It is a separate space filled with liquid.
notes.3: Vacuoles do not produce energy. They are spaces filled with cell sap or other liquid.

explain: Vacuoles are storage bags inside cells. Plant cells have one big vacuole. Animal cells have small ones or none.

notes.0: Size is not the reason. Many animals are larger than many plants. Think about how plants and animals get their food.
notes.2: Animal cells do not have a cell wall. Think about what chloroplasts do and whether animals need that.
notes.3: Chloroplasts are not too big for animal cells. Think about how animals get their food compared with plants.

why.right: Plant cells have chloroplasts because plants make their own food by photosynthesis using light energy.
wrong: Plant cells have chloroplasts because plants are larger and need bigger cell parts than animals.
Plant cells have chloroplasts because the cell wall must be filled with green material to stay stiff.

explain: Plants make their own food through photosynthesis. Animals eat other things for food, so they don't need chloroplasts.

notes.0: Growth is controlled by the nucleus. Without it, the cell cannot grow.
notes.1: Making food is controlled by the nucleus too. Removing the nucleus would not increase food making.
notes.3: Losing the nucleus does not turn a cell into an animal cell. Animal cells also need a nucleus. Think about what the nucleus does.

why.right: A cell without a nucleus dies because nothing is left to control its activities and growth.
wrong: A cell without a nucleus dies because all its cytoplasm leaks out through the gap.
A cell without a nucleus dies because the cell wall collapses with nothing to hold it up.

explain: The nucleus controls everything the cell does. Without it, the cell cannot survive or function.

notes.0: Only plant cells have a cell wall. Animal cells have only a cell membrane on the outside.
notes.1: Only plant cells have chloroplasts, because only plants make their own food.
notes.3: Plant and animal cells share some parts but not all. Plant cells have extra parts that animal cells lack.

explain: Both plant and animal cells have these basic parts. But plant cells also have a cell wall and chloroplasts.

notes.0: Animal cells are not always bigger, and size is not the main difference. Think about which parts each type of cell has.
notes.2: Most plant and animal cells have one nucleus each. Think about parts that only one type of cell has.
notes.3: There are clear differences in the parts that the two types of cell contain.

explain: Plant cells have a rigid cell wall and chloroplasts for making food. Animal cells have neither of these.

notes.0: Plant cells are not frozen. Their shape comes from a layer that animal cells do not have.
notes.2: Animal cells can hold a shape, but it is flexible. Think about the extra outer layer that plant cells have.
notes.3: The age of a cell does not decide its shape. Think about the extra outer layer in plant cells.

why.right: Plant cells have a fixed shape because a rigid cell wall surrounds each cell.
wrong: Plant cells have a fixed shape because a thick cell membrane hardens around each cell.
Plant cells have a fixed shape because a large nucleus fills up most of each cell.

explain: The cell wall is tough and rigid. It prevents the plant cell from changing shape. Animal cells have only a flexible membrane.

notes.0: Red blood cells come from animals, including humans. Look for the parts that only plant cells have.
notes.1: Nerve cells carry signals in animals. They have no cell wall or chloroplasts.
notes.3: Muscle cells are found in animals and have no cell wall. Look for parts found only in plant cells.

why.right: A leaf cell is identified as a plant cell because it has a cell wall and chloroplasts, which animal cells lack.
wrong: A leaf cell is identified as a plant cell because it has a nucleus, which animal cells lack.
A leaf cell is identified as a plant cell because it has a cell membrane, which animal cells lack.

explain: Plant cells have a cell wall on the outside and chloroplasts inside. This combination is unique to plants.

notes.0: Trees and flowers are plants, so they are made of plant cells.
notes.2: Animal cells are not found only in water. Many animals live on land and are made of animal cells too.
notes.3: Rocks are not living, so they are not made of cells.

explain: Animal cells are found in all animals, including humans. They make up our skin, blood, muscles and organs.

notes.0: Not every plant cell has chloroplasts. Think about plant parts that grow where there is no light.
notes.1: Leaves have the most chloroplasts, but green stems have them too. The question is about parts that receive no light.
notes.3: Chloroplasts are found in plant cells, not animal cells. The question is whether every plant cell has them.

why.right: Root cells have no chloroplasts because roots grow underground, where no light reaches them for photosynthesis.
wrong: Root cells have no chloroplasts because roots take in ready-made food from the soil instead.
Root cells have no chloroplasts because their cell walls are too thick for chloroplasts to fit inside.

explain: Chloroplasts need light to work. Root cells underground have no light, so they don't have chloroplasts.

notes.0: Red is not the colour of chloroplasts. Think about the colour of most leaves.
notes.2: Yellow is not the usual colour. Healthy leaves get their colour from the pigment in chloroplasts.
notes.3: Chloroplasts are not clear. They contain a coloured pigment that gives leaves their colour.

why.right: Chloroplasts look green because they contain chlorophyll, a green pigment that absorbs light.
wrong: Chloroplasts look green because they are filled with green cell sap from the vacuole.
Chloroplasts look green because the cell wall around them is coloured green.

explain: Chlorophyll is a green pigment inside chloroplasts. This is what makes leaves green and captures sunlight.

notes.0: Plant cells need a nucleus to control their activities. Think of one special animal cell that loses its nucleus.
notes.1: Most animal cells need a nucleus to survive. The answer is one special type of cell.
notes.3: Most cells die without a nucleus. Only certain special cells can manage without one.

why.right: Mature red blood cells survive without a nucleus because their job of carrying oxygen does not need one.
wrong: Mature red blood cells survive without a nucleus because their cell wall controls the cell instead.
Mature red blood cells survive without a nucleus because they make their own food using chloroplasts.

explain: Mature red blood cells push out their nucleus before entering the bloodstream. They can still deliver oxygen without it.

notes.0: Animal cells have no rigid outer layer to hold a square shape. Think about what their outer layer is like.
notes.1: A box-like shape comes from a cell wall, which animal cells do not have.
notes.3: A few cells, such as nerve cells, have long branches, but most animal cells are not star-shaped.

why.right: Most animal cells are round or irregular because they have only a flexible cell membrane and no cell wall.
wrong: Most animal cells are round or irregular because their cell wall is soft and bends easily.
Most animal cells are round or irregular because their large vacuole pushes evenly in all directions.

explain: Animal cells do not have a rigid cell wall, so they can be round or irregular in shape. Plant cells have a cell wall that gives them a fixed shape.

notes.0: Animal cells have neither a cell wall nor chloroplasts.
notes.2: Bacteria have a cell wall but no chloroplasts. The cell in the question has both parts.
notes.3: Fungal cells have a cell wall but no chloroplasts, because fungi cannot make their own food.

why.right: A cell with both a cell wall and chloroplasts is a plant cell because only plant cells have both parts.
wrong: A cell with both a cell wall and chloroplasts is a plant cell because only plant cells have a cell wall.
A cell with both a cell wall and chloroplasts is a plant cell because only plant cells have a nucleus.

explain: Only plant cells have both a cell wall and chloroplasts. This combination is a clear sign of a plant cell.

notes.0: Plant cells usually have one large central vacuole. Animal cells are different here.
notes.2: Animal cells do not have more or bigger vacuoles than plant cells. Compare them with the large central vacuole of a plant cell.
notes.3: Vacuoles are found in many plant cells, not only in roots. The question compares animal cells with plant cells.

explain: Plant cells have one big central vacuole. Animal cells have tiny ones or no vacuoles at all.

notes.0: Size is not what 'unicellular' describes. Think about what 'uni' means in a word like 'unicycle'.
notes.2: An organism with many organs is made of many cells. 'Uni' means one.
notes.3: Unicellular organisms are alive. The word describes how many cells the organism has.

explain: Unicellular means 'one cell.' Examples are bacteria and amoeba. They are alive but have only one cell.

notes.1: Multicellular organisms are alive. The word describes how many cells make up the organism.
notes.2: Size is not what the word describes. 'Multi' means many.
notes.3: Age is not what the word describes. Think about what 'multi' means.

explain: Multicellular organisms have many cells that work together. Humans, plants, and animals are all multicellular.

notes.0: A human is made of trillions of cells. Look for an organism made of a single cell.
notes.1: A dog is made of many cells working together. Look for an organism whose whole body is one cell.
notes.3: A tree is made of many cells forming tissues and organs. Look for an organism made of one cell.

why.right: A bacterium is unicellular because its whole body is one cell that carries out every life process.
wrong: A bacterium is unicellular because it is too small to be seen without a microscope.
A bacterium is unicellular because it has no nucleus and so cannot divide into more cells.

explain: Bacteria are made of just one cell. Humans, dogs, and trees are made of millions of cells.

notes.0: Most unicellular organisms are far smaller than the eye can see. Think about how small one cell is.
notes.2: Whether something can be seen does not depend on the day. It depends on the size of the organism.
notes.3: Size is what decides whether something can be seen with the naked eye. Think about how small a single cell is.

why.right: Most unicellular organisms need a microscope to be seen because a single cell is too small for the eye.
wrong: Most unicellular organisms need a microscope to be seen because they move too quickly for the eye.
Most unicellular organisms need a microscope to be seen because they live only inside other organisms.

explain: Most unicellular organisms are microscopic (very tiny). You need a microscope to see them.

notes.0: In everyday English a tissue is a piece of paper, but in biology the word has a different meaning linked to cells.
notes.2: A tissue is not one cell. It is made of many cells.
notes.3: No part of a microscope is called a tissue. In biology the word is about how cells are grouped.

explain: A tissue is made of many similar cells. For example, muscle tissue is made of many muscle cells working together.

notes.0: In everyday English an organ is a musical instrument, but in biology the word means a body structure such as the heart.
notes.2: An organ is much larger than one cell. It is built from more than one kind of tissue.
notes.3: No microscope is called an organ. In biology, the heart and the stomach are examples of organs.

explain: An organ is made of several types of tissue. Your heart is an organ made of muscle, nerve, and blood vessel tissue.

notes.0: In a multicellular organism, cells are specialised. A muscle cell cannot carry oxygen like a red blood cell does.
notes.2: No single cell controls the whole body. Each cell has its own nucleus.
notes.3: Cells in the body depend on each other. Think about how nerve, muscle and blood cells each help the body.

why.right: A multicellular organism works because its cells are specialised for different jobs and work together.
wrong: A multicellular organism works because every cell carries out every job by itself.
A multicellular organism works because one large cell controls all the other cells.

explain: Your body has trillions of cells. Different cells specialise in different jobs and work together to keep you alive.

notes.0: Cells in a healthy body do not fight each other. 'Labour' here means work.
notes.2: Cells are not separated. Division of labour describes how the work is shared out.
notes.3: Cells of all sizes do work. The term describes how different jobs are shared between cells.

explain: In your body, muscle cells contract, nerve cells send signals, and blood cells carry oxygen. Each type has its own job.

notes.0: Appearance is not a scientific reason. Think about what many cells can do that one cell cannot.
notes.2: Strength and speed are not the main point. Think about how many cells can share out different jobs.
notes.3: There is a good reason. Think about how different cells in the body do different jobs.

why.right: Multicellular organisms have many cells because different cells can specialise in different jobs.
wrong: Multicellular organisms have many cells because small cells are always stronger than large cells.
Multicellular organisms have many cells because one giant cell would be too heavy to move.

explain: Many cells allow each type of cell to be specialised for one job. A single giant cell could not carry out all these jobs as well.

notes.0: An organ is made of tissues, so tissues must come before organs.
notes.2: A tissue is made of cells, so cells must come before tissues.
notes.3: This order runs from largest to smallest. The question asks for smallest to largest.

why.right: Living things are organised from small to large because cells form tissues, tissues form organs and organs form the organism.
wrong: Living things are organised from small to large because cells form organs, organs form tissues and tissues form the organism.
Living things are organised from small to large because tissues form cells, cells form organs and organs form the organism.

explain: Cells group together to form tissues. Different tissues form organs. Organs work together to make up the whole organism.

notes.0: Cells do not have feelings such as boredom. Think about what the body needs new cells for.
notes.2: Laziness is not a scientific reason. Think about what new cells are used for in the body.
notes.3: Cells do divide. A cut that heals shows that new cells are being made.

why.right: Cells divide because new cells are needed for growth, for repairing damage and for reproduction.
wrong: Cells divide because a cell that grows too old splits apart before it dies.
Cells divide because the nucleus breaks into pieces when the cell becomes too full.

explain: Cell division allows organisms to grow, repair injuries, and reproduce. One cell becomes two identical cells.

notes.0: The cell does not disappear. Think about what happens to the nucleus first and what the cell becomes.
notes.2: A cell growing bigger is not cell division. Division ends with more cells than at the start.
notes.3: Cell division is important. Think about how a cut heals or how a person grows.

why.right: Cell division gives two cells because the nucleus divides first and then the cytoplasm splits in two.
wrong: Cell division gives two cells because the cell membrane splits while the nucleus stays whole.
Cell division gives two cells because two old cells join and then split apart again.

explain: The nucleus divides first. Then the cytoplasm splits. You end up with two cells where you started with one.

notes.0: One cell dividing does not leave just one cell. Think about what happens when something splits in half.
notes.1: One division does not give three cells. A cell splits once, into equal parts.
notes.3: Cell division is not random. One division gives a fixed number of cells.

explain: When a cell divides, it creates two daughter cells. Each one is identical to the original cell.

notes.0: The nucleus does not simply disappear. Each new cell needs the information it holds.
notes.2: Shrinking would not help. Each new cell needs its own set of the information in the nucleus.
notes.3: Moving position does not help the new cells. Think about what each new cell needs from the nucleus.

why.right: The nucleus copies its DNA before division so that each new cell gets a full set of instructions.
wrong: The nucleus copies its DNA before division so that the new cells can grow twice as large.
The nucleus copies its DNA before division so that the cytoplasm can be split in half.

explain: Before dividing, the nucleus makes a complete copy of all its DNA. This way, each new cell has the same instructions.

notes.0: Cells are not lazy. Think about what happens to the number of cells when cells divide.
notes.2: Cell division does not stop growth. Think about what dividing does to the number of cells.
notes.3: Growth depends on cell division. A baby grows into an adult because of it.

why.right: Organisms grow because cell division increases the number of cells in the body.
wrong: Organisms grow because each cell keeps getting bigger without ever dividing.
Organisms grow because cell division joins small cells together into large cells.

explain: You grew from a baby to your current size because your cells kept dividing. More cells make a bigger body.

notes.0: Most body cells cannot keep dividing without end. They stop after a certain number of divisions.
notes.2: Animal cells can also divide many times. The answer applies to most cells, not only one type.
notes.3: Colour has nothing to do with cell division. Think about whether most cells can keep dividing without stopping.

explain: Most body cells can divide only a limited number of times. After that, they stop dividing and are eventually replaced by other cells.

notes.0: Broken bones are repaired by cell division, but they are not the only damage repaired this way. Check the other options as well.
notes.1: Cuts in the skin are repaired by cell division, but other damage is repaired in the same way.
notes.2: Burned skin is repaired by cell division, but so are other kinds of damage.

why.right: Cell division repairs many kinds of damage because it makes new cells to replace damaged ones.
wrong: Cell division repairs only skin cuts because skin is the only tissue whose cells can divide.
Cell division repairs only broken bones because bone cells are the only cells with a nucleus.

explain: Cell division helps your body repair many types of damage by creating new healthy cells to replace damaged ones.

notes.0: This does not describe how it happens. In asexual reproduction only one parent is involved and no mating takes place.
notes.2: Cells fighting is not reproduction. Reproduction makes new organisms.
notes.3: Eating other cells is feeding, not reproduction. Think about how one cell can become two.

explain: When bacteria or amoebas divide, each parent cell becomes two identical offspring. No mating is needed.

notes.0: Cells do not make noise. Think about what too many extra cells do to the organs around them.
notes.2: Cancer cells divide too fast, not too slowly. Think about what a growing lump of cells does to nearby organs.
notes.3: Cancer is dangerous. Think about what happens when cells keep dividing when they should not.

why.right: Cancer is dangerous because cells that divide out of control form tumours that damage nearby tissues.
wrong: Cancer is dangerous because cells that divide out of control use up all the oxygen in the air.
Cancer is dangerous because cells that divide out of control stop all other cells from dividing.

explain: Cancer happens when cells divide when they should not. This creates tumours that damage healthy tissue.

notes.0: Junk food lacks many nutrients that cells need. Think about what cells need to work and divide properly.
notes.2: Sitting in the dark does not help cells. Think about food, exercise and sleep.
notes.3: Some choices do affect cells. Smoking and too much sun can damage them.

why.right: A healthy lifestyle helps cells because they get the nutrients they need and less damage from smoke and sunlight.
wrong: A healthy lifestyle helps cells because exercise makes every cell in the body divide much faster.
A healthy lifestyle helps cells because smoke and strong sunlight give them more energy to divide.

explain: A healthy lifestyle gives your cells what they need to function properly and divide correctly when needed.

notes.0: The microscope's value was not about making glass look nice. Think about what people could see with it for the first time.
notes.2: Microscopes did not replace magnifying glasses. They allowed much smaller things to be seen.
notes.3: The microscope was very important. Before it, nobody knew that cells existed.

why.right: The microscope was important because cells are too small to be seen with the eye alone.
wrong: The microscope was important because it made cells grow large enough to be seen.
The microscope was important because it was the first tool ever to use glass lenses.

explain: Before microscopes, people didn't know cells existed. Microscopes opened up an entire hidden world.

notes.0: Both microscopes are used for science, not for making things look pretty. Think about how much each one can magnify.
notes.2: Electron microscopes do not use sunlight. They use beams of electrons.
notes.3: All machines can break down. Think about how much each microscope can magnify.

why.right: An electron microscope shows more detail because it magnifies far more than a light microscope.
wrong: An electron microscope shows more detail because it uses brighter sunlight than a light microscope.
An electron microscope shows more detail because it makes the specimen grow bigger before viewing.

explain: Electron microscopes can magnify up to about 500 000 times. Light microscopes magnify only up to about 1500 times, so electron microscopes show much more detail.

notes.0: Microscopes showed that cells are real. They became visible for the first time.
notes.2: Cells are not made of rock. Cells are the living units of organisms.
notes.3: Something new was discovered. Think about what scientists saw in every living sample they looked at.

explain: Scientists found that all living things are made of cells. This idea is called the cell theory.

notes.0: Scientists do not ignore cells. Many diseases are caused by changes in cells.
notes.2: Cells cannot be turned into robots. Scientists study cells using microscopes and by growing them.
notes.3: Scientists do study cells to learn about diseases. Think about the tools they use.

why.right: Studying cells helps scientists understand diseases because many diseases cause changes inside cells.
wrong: Studying cells helps scientists understand diseases because diseased cells are the only cells that can be seen.
Studying cells helps scientists understand diseases because diseased cells always look the same as healthy cells.

explain: Studying cells helps doctors understand how diseases work and develop medicines and treatments.

notes.0: A vaccine is not food. It works with the body's immune system to prevent disease.
notes.2: A vaccine has nothing to do with microscopes. It protects the body against disease.
notes.3: A vaccine is not a cell. It is a substance given to prepare the body against a disease.

explain: A vaccine helps the body's immune cells learn to recognise and fight a disease before the person catches it. This protects the person from the disease.

notes.0: Microscopes have changed a lot. Early ones had simple lenses. Think about what modern ones can show.
notes.2: Speed is not how microscopes are compared. Think about how small the things are that they can show.
notes.3: Modern microscopes are not worse. Think about the electron microscope compared with early lenses.

explain: From simple lenses to electron microscopes, technology keeps improving. We keep discovering more about cells.

notes.0: A biopsy is a medical test, not something done for fun. Think about what doctors look for in cells.
notes.2: A biopsy takes cells out of the body. Think about what doctors check for.
notes.3: A biopsy has a clear purpose. Doctors study the cells to find out whether there is a disease.

why.right: Doctors examine biopsies because changes seen in cells under a microscope show whether a disease is present.
wrong: Doctors examine biopsies because removing a few cells is enough to cure the disease.
Doctors examine biopsies because diseased cells grow large enough to be seen without a microscope.

explain: By examining cells from a biopsy, doctors can diagnose diseases and figure out the best treatment.

notes.0: Cloning is not about dirt. It is about making an organism with the same genetic information as another.
notes.2: Cloning does not break things. It makes a copy of an organism.
notes.3: Seeds usually come from two parents, so the offspring differ from each parent. Cloning uses the genetic information of only one organism.

explain: Scientists can take one cell and use its DNA to create an organism that is genetically identical to the original.

notes.0: Stem cells are found in animals, including humans, as well as in plants. Think about what is special about these cells.
notes.2: Stem cell research is biology, not making clothes. It studies a special kind of cell.
notes.3: Stem cell research is about living cells, not robots. Think about cells that are not yet specialised.

explain: Stem cells can grow into many different types of cells. Scientists hope to use them to treat injuries and diseases.

notes.0: Cell technology is widely used in medicine. Think about where scientists test new medicines first.
notes.2: Cells are not ignored in medicine. Many medicines are tested on cells grown in labs.
notes.3: Animal and human cells are studied too, not only plant cells.

explain: Cell cultures in labs let scientists test thousands of drug compounds quickly before trying them on patients.
